top_authentic_signals.name: Thermal Noise & Sensor Consistency
top_authentic_signals.summary: The image shows consistent, subtle grain in nearly all regions (4.4% smooth blocks, variance 4206.7) - the expected fingerprint of a real camera sensor.
top_authentic_signals.what_found: Only 4.4% of pixel blocks are flat - the rest carry a consistent, fine-grained texture at the sub-pixel level. This is the natural noise floor left by photon shot noise and thermal read noise on real camera sensors. The variance of 4206.7 is healthy: present but controlled, suggesting base-ISO capture with standard noise reduction.
top_authentic_signals.why_it_matters: Uniform, subtle grain that's present everywhere but never overwhelming is genuinely difficult for AI to replicate convincingly. This pattern - real grain without being suspiciously chaotic - is one of the stronger authentic fingerprints this test can find.
top_authentic_signals.caveat: Heavy compression, denoising, upscaling, or added grain filters can all change the noise profile independently of whether the image was generated or photographed.

top_ai_signals.why_it_matters: When an image has broken anatomy, impossible geometry, or missing shadows, that is strong evidence it was generated rather than photographed.
top_ai_signals.caveat: This detector is useful, but it can still be wrong and should be treated as one part of the full picture.

This balanced exposure is realistic-looking but not diagnostic - it fits equally well for a careful real photograph and a modern AI generator.
top_inconclusive_signals.why_it_matters: Lighting is most useful when it's either suspiciously perfect (AI) or clearly clipping (real). A balanced middle-ground doesn't give us enough to work with, so this signal defers to others.
top_inconclusive_signals.caveat: HDR post-processing, tone mapping, strong flash, and professional retouching can all alter exposure profiles - introducing 'AI-like' qualities into real photos or vice versa.
